title: Deconstruct, Analyze, Rebuild — Additional Real-Game Observation

scenes.title: Similar Features, Different Decisions
lines: In these new examples, look for a decision rather than a feature name.
Into the Breach shows movement cells and enemy attack directions together.
The question is what to protect and where to move, beyond simply moving forward.
In Noita, notice how terrain and nearby materials change after a projectile passes.
Watching damage alone and watching the route left afterward are different observations.
One fire button may involve both a target and an approach route.
Copying the striking effect does not automatically create those choices.
Record the information you saw, the action you chose, and the result left on screen.
The original small diagram is a starting point for combining them into your own rule.

scenes.title: Choose One Action from Actual Play
lines: Choose just one movement and attack in Into the Breach.
Separate reading the attack direction, moving the mech, and the changed enemy position.
Writing only 'hit an enemy' can miss how displacement changes the next situation.
In Noita, observe one projectile's path instead of the entire exploration.
What was the target, what changed, and where could the character move afterward?
In FTL, observe the ship's rooms, crew, and power indicators together.
Choose one immediate state to attend to instead of the broad feature 'control a ship.'
You do not need to cut every game into an equal duration.
Find a moment that includes the information before a choice and its result afterward.

scenes.title: Turn an Observation into a Testable Question
lines: Record visible changes separately from your explanation of the fun.
A changed piece of terrain in Noita is an observable event.
'I liked having a new route' is an idea you want to investigate.
Separate the number of routes from the new option to avoid danger.
FTL's power and room states can be observed in the same way.
Was the appeal the amount of information, or having several needs at once?
An edited introduction cannot establish a player's thoughts or the internal code.
Bring the question it raises into the original controlled test.
Keep the feeling while making the condition you compare smaller.

scenes.title: Connect a Commercial Example to a Controlled Test
lines: FTL shows several rooms and state indicators during a battle.
It can prompt a question about which information to check first.
Two different battles edited together are not a controlled comparison.
If enemies, ships and equipment all change, several factors may explain a difference.
The original jump test changed only the platform width or restart wait.
Keeping other factors fixed makes the changed condition easier to examine.
For a material-rich world like Noita, a small experiment might begin with one material.
Use the striking example to find a question and the small test to investigate it.
Connecting their roles turns observation into design work.

scenes.title: Keep the Decision, Change the Situation
lines: When making another game, more than the scene's appearance can be retained.
A position choice in Into the Breach asks which cells will be affected next.
Noita's changing space can prompt a prediction about the route left after an action.
This does not make the two games' rules identical.
Choose the decision of predicting an outcome and put it into another test situation.
A moving-door game or a light-timing game can also ask that question.
FTL's competing needs might become a choice of where to send limited help first.
New rules can be tested without borrowing the original game's name or artwork.
Ask actual players whether that decision works in the new situation.

scenes.title: Leave a Design Record of One Moment
lines: Finally, organize the notes you can leave after observing an actual scene.
For Into the Breach, record a position choice after reading an attack direction.
For Noita, observe the environmental change and what remains for the next movement.
For FTL, record which simultaneous state you wanted to attend to first.
Then choose one small condition that could investigate that explanation.
Show the changed test and ask where the player looked and when they decided.
An idea from a trailer and an actual player's answer are different evidence.
If they differ, find the missed information or result before adding more features.
Observing, testing and rebuilding helps you create rules for your own game.
